This parallel between the verbal and visual memory literatures is novel because, to date, despite multiple attempts, no empirical study has definitively demonstrated a testing effect for purely visual, asemantic information without concern that participants are instead using some form of re-coded semantic information to support their memory responses.
Participants were undergraduate students from the University of Colorado Boulder who participated in the study for course credit.

Participants for all studies were recruited from the same pool of undergraduates -students enrolled in the Introduction to Psychology course at CU Boulder, participating through CU Boulder's Sona system, a cloud-based software application used to manage the research participant pool.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A reasonable expectation for a testing effect study is a mean d' difference between conditions of 0.3, with a d' standard deviation of approximately 0.8. Obtaining 80% power to detect this effect in a repeated-measures design using a two-tailed paired t-test (alpha 0.05) requires around 58 participants. We targeted approximately this number in each study, with exact totals depending on how many participants signed up in the last 1-2 days of the experiment, through CU Boulder's Sona system. For Experiment 7, we had many more participants for two reasons: (1) we collected fewer trials per participant resulting in a greater d' standard deviation, and (2) we ran three versions of the study that were not originally meant to be combined and were instead meant to be comparison between two halves of the experiment, but afterwards found a coding mistake in half of the experiment for the first two versions; we discarded the data from the halves with the coding mistake, and we combined the otherwise equivalent halves that suffered no error.

In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. We ran automated data-quality checks on 1402 columns; 13 columns have at least one potential issue (13 columns with numeric values stored as text).

live_data_statements: This parallel between the verbal and visual memory literatures is novel because, to date, despite multiple attempts, no empirical study has definitively demonstrated a testing effect for purely visual, asemantic information without concern that participants are instead using some form of re-coded semantic information to support their memory responses.
Participants were undergraduate students from the University of Colorado Boulder who participated in the study for course credit.

Participants for all studies were recruited from the same pool of undergraduates -students enrolled in the Introduction to Psychology course at CU Boulder, participating through CU Boulder's Sona system, a cloud-based software application used to manage the research participant pool.
All participants gave informed consent according to procedures approved by the
We targeted approximately this number in each study, with exact totals depending on how many participants signed up in the last 1-2 days of the experiment, through CU Boulder's Sona system.
Next, half of the images underwent retrieval practice, in which participants were presented with a restricted circular aperture to cue their memory of the whole item (Fig. 1).

Next, to measure the efficacy of retrieval from this partial cue, participants were shown a whole object missing a circular patch in the same location used for the aperture cue (a "holepunch image", Fig. 1) and were asked if this was the correct whole object matching the aperture presented immediately prior.
Sixty-three undergraduate students completed the study; seven were excluded because they failed to respond on more than 20% of trials.

These six similar exemplars were exploited in the experimental design to ensure that participants were learning and retrieving visual details, rather than relying on semantic information or verbal labels.

That is, if participants had been shown only two yellow chairs, they might have used a simple scheme such as "squat chair" versus "tall chair," but with six stimuli sharing the same name, easy verbal differentiation between all stimuli was precluded.
Middle top: Half of studied items undergo retrieval practice, in which participants are prompted with a word cue to remember the whole image that was paired with that word.
Sixty CU Boulder undergraduate students completed the study; no participants were excluded.

Second, for retrieval practice and final test, instead of cuing memory with an aperture, participants were cued with a word and asked how well they could remember the image that was paired with that word, rating their memory from 1 to 3.

In this paradigm, instead of part-to-whole pattern completion, participants were cued via an arbitrary association from a previously paired word to the object, which did not produce a learning benefit.
Sixty-eight undergraduate students completed the experiment; 6 were excluded because they failed to respond on more than 20% of trials.
Fifty-eight undergraduate students completed the study; 6 were excluded because they failed to respond on more than 20% of trials.

Thirty-two of the participants were female, 26 were male; 6 were Hispanic/Latine and 52 not Hispanic/Latino; 1 participant was American Indian/Alaskan Native, 8 Asian, 1 African American, 1 Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, 46
Sixty-seven undergraduate students completed the study; 4 were excluded because they failed to respond on more than 20% of trials.
Thirty-nine of the participants were female, 28 were male; 5 Hispanic/Latino, 59 not Hispanic/Latino; 1 American Indian/Alaskan Native, 9
At final test, participants were first shown an aperture and asked how well they remembered the whole image it came from (not shown here, see Fig. 2).

Next, the aperture disappeared from view and participants were immediately shown an array containing all six exemplars from that stimulus group (e.g., "red lawnmowers"), each with a patch corresponding to the location of the just-seen aperture removed from the image (i.e., "holepunch" images).
Participants were prompted to select the lawnmower from which they believed the just-seen aperture had been drawn.
Second, at final test, instead of the single match/mismatch probe, participants were presented with an aperture followed by a 6-alternative forced choice (6-AFC) recognition task (Fig. 11).
Sixty-Two undergraduate students completed the study; 10 were excluded because they failed to respond on more than 20% of trials.
Forty-seven of the participants were female, 14 male, 1 chose not to answer.
Fifteen of the participants were Hispanic/Latino, 44 not Hispanic/Latino; 4 were American Indian/Alaskan Native, 5 Asian, 50 White, and 3 chose not to answer.
Experiment 7 used the same aperture-cued visual memory task as Experiment 1 but modified the restudy condition so that participants were shown information about the future retrieval cue.
Two hundred and forty-two undergraduate students completed the study; 5 were excluded for failing to respond on more than 20% of trials.

One hundred and seventy-five of the participants were female, 61 male, and 1 other; 34 were Hispanic/Latino and 201 not Hispanic/Latino, 2 chose not to answer; 2 were American Indian/Alaskan Native, 22 Asian, 7 black/African American, 196 White, and 10 chose not to answer.

More participants were recruited than in earlier experiments because there were fewer trials per condition than in Experiments 3 through 6 (which each included 8 test blocks), and because our intention had been to look for an interaction between task type and study condition, which may have required more data to detect.

Furthermore, even if exposure time for the aperture were the more important factor (although it is not clear why this would be the case under an account in terms of simple exposure), which would suggest an exposure advantage for retrieval practice trials, this advantage should be offset by the fact that, on mismatch trials, participants were exposed to the wrong "holepunch" image (the lure, not the target) for 3s, providing interference.
Middle top: Half of studied items undergo retrieval practice, in which a peephole aperture from the original object is shown and participants are prompted to remember the whole image.
At final test, participants were first shown an aperture and asked how well they remembered the whole image it came from (not shown here, see Fig.2).

text.text: Recognizing a partially occluded object is typically effortless and automatic: visual cortex fills in the missing parts to infer a recognizable whole.
We investigated whether this process of visual pattern completion constitutes not just a retrieval operation, but also a learning mechanism.
Participants studied whole objects, after which each object was assigned either to retrieval practice, cued by a circular aperture offering a "peephole" view, or to restudy.
At final test, retrieval-practiced (peephole-cued) objects were better remembered than restudied objects, demonstrating a visual testing effect.
Crucially, targets and lures were highly visually similar and shared the same verbal-conceptual identity, requiring memory for fine-grained visual detail rather than conceptual information.
This demonstrates that retrieval practice can enhance visual memory without requiring semantic mediation, challenging prominent theories of the testing effect.
Moreover, when retrieval no longer required pattern completion-retrieval without a peephole cue-the testing effect was significantly reduced.

Together, these findings reveal that visual pattern completion not only retrieves perceptual representations but also strengthens them, identifying a mechanism of retrieval-based learning that extends beyond the verbal and conceptual domains.

The ability to recognize partially occluded objects is a signature achievement of human vision.

In recent years, even though the capabilities of deep neural networks on many object recognition measures have approached and surpassed those of humans (He et al., 2015; Tsirtsakis et al., 2025), human vision continues to exhibit greater robustness than many artificial vision models under challenging conditions of partial occlusion (Kassaw et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In recent years, even though the capabilities of deep neural networks on many object recognition measures have approached and surpassed those of humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(He et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Tsirtsakis et al., 2025)</ref>, human vision continues to exhibit greater robustness than many artificial vision models under challenging conditions of partial occlusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kassaw et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Even when an object is partially hidden or visually degraded, human observers can often identify it rapidly and effortlessly.

This ability is presumed to be supported by visual pattern completion, a process in which visual cortex infers missing features from stored object representations to reconstruct a coherent whole (Brown & Koch, 2000; Kosai et al., 2014; Lee, 2003; Lerner et al., 2002; Tang et al., 2014 Tang et al., , 2018)).
text.formatted: This ability is presumed to be supported by visual pattern completion, a process in which visual cortex infers missing features from stored object representations to reconstruct a coherent whole <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Brown & Koch, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kosai et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Lee, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lerner et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Tang et al., 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Tang et al., , 2018))</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, pattern completion improves if the observer has previously been exposed to the specific whole object that is later presented in degraded form (Gabrieli et al., 1994; Gollin, 1960; Gorlin et al., 2012; Warrington & Weiskrantz, 1968), which suggests that the process not only draws on general visual object knowledge, but also serves as a key retrieval mechanism in visual memory.
text.formatted: Furthermore, pattern completion improves if the observer has previously been exposed to the specific whole object that is later presented in degraded form <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Gabrieli et al., 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Gollin, 1960;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Gorlin et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Warrington & Weiskrantz, 1968)</ref>, which suggests that the process not only draws on general visual object knowledge, but also serves as a key retrieval mechanism in visual memory.

text.text: In this study, we propose that the role of visual pattern completion extends beyond the retrieval operation involved in occluded object recognition: we ask whether the process of "filling in" the missing visual information also serves as a learning mechanism, more powerful than simple visual exposure, that strengthens the representations that are being retrieved.
If visual occlusion is important for visual learning, this has fundamental implications for theories of visual learning and it also suggests a novel parallel between visual and verbal memory.

In studies of memory for verbal material, retrieval practice reliably produces superior long-term retention than simple restudy -a phenomenon termed the "testing effect" (Karpicke & Roediger, 2008; Roediger III & Karpicke, 2006).
text.formatted: In studies of memory for verbal material, retrieval practice reliably produces superior long-term retention than simple restudy -a phenomenon termed the "testing effect" <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Karpicke & Roediger, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Roediger III & Karpicke, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Here we suggest that the ubiquitous examples of occlusion encountered in our visual environment provide the visual system with retrieval practice.

The analogy is well matched: in verbal testing effect studies, retrieval practice is typically followed by feedback; in the visual environment, as we move our heads or as objects move, previously occluded objects emerge into un-occluded view, effectively providing feedback.
We predict that visual pattern completion followed by feedback enhances memory more than simply experiencing additional exposure to the whole object (learning from an unoccluded view).
An empirical demonstration of this would amount to a visual testing effect.

This parallel between the verbal and visual memory literatures is novel because, to date, despite multiple attempts, no empirical study has definitively demonstrated a testing effect for purely visual, asemantic information without concern that participants are instead using some form of re-coded semantic information to support their memory responses.

Demonstrating this empirically is difficult: one approach is to attempt to use abstract visual material that is unlikely to engage conceptual representations; another is to design a memory task in which conceptual representations cannot be useful even if they are engaged.
The present study is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to exploit both of these approaches together.

Prior studies have examined the effects of retrieval practice for visual materials, and we propose that they fall into three groups: studies that used neither approach outlined above, studies that used the former approach (reducing conceptual information) but not the latter, and studies that used the latter approach (employing a task that renders conceptual representations unhelpful) but not the former.

In the first group of studies, the stimuli were visual, but they possessed conceptual information or could be verbally labelled, making it possible for verbal/conceptual representations to support task performance.

For example, Mercer and Jones (2019) used a recognition paradigm and found a benefit of retrieval practice over restudy for visual images, but the images were objects that could be easily named (e.g., binoculars, melon).
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Mercer and Jones (2019)</ref> used a recognition paradigm and found a benefit of retrieval practice over restudy for visual images, but the images were objects that could be easily named (e.g., binoculars, melon).

text.text: Other studies in this group used associative recall of visual material and found testing effects but, again, one or both items in the learned pair possessed conceptual or verbal information, for example: English words paired with Chinese characters in non-Chinese readers (Kang, 2010); novel locations of meaningful features (e.g., river, road) on a map (Carpenter & Pashler, 2007); the silhouettes of nameable objects paired with arbitrary colors (Schuetze et al., 2019; Sutterer & Awh, 2016); face-name pairs (Carpenter & DeLosh, 2005; Morris & Fritz, 2000; Tse et al., 2010); bird images paired with bird family names (Siler & Benjamin, 2020); word-image pairs (Lifanov et al., 2021); and scene-object pairs (Jonker et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Other studies in this group used associative recall of visual material and found testing effects but, again, one or both items in the learned pair possessed conceptual or verbal information, for example: English words paired with Chinese characters in non-Chinese readers <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Kang, 2010)</ref>; novel locations of meaningful features (e.g., river, road) on a map <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Carpenter & Pashler, 2007)</ref>; the silhouettes of nameable objects paired with arbitrary colors <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Schuetze et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Sutterer & Awh, 2016)</ref>; face-name pairs <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Carpenter & DeLosh, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Morris & Fritz, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Tse et al., 2010)</ref>; bird images paired with bird family names <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Siler & Benjamin, 2020)</ref>; word-image pairs <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Lifanov et al., 2021)</ref>; and scene-object pairs <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Jonker et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: As such, for this set of studies, it is not clear if the results reflect a pure visual testing effect or if, instead, the learning benefits of visual retrieval practice were mediated by verbal recoding of one or both items in the pair, and the use of conceptual associations.
Two studies fall into the second group, in which the authors attempted to demonstrate a purely visual testing effect by reducing or eliminating the conceptual content of the stimuli.

First, Ferreira & Wimber (2023) found a visual testing effect for words paired with nameable objects, but not for words paired with meaningless squiggles, supporting the hypothesis that a testing effect requires some form of semantic content.
text.formatted: First, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Ferreira & Wimber (2023)</ref> found a visual testing effect for words paired with nameable objects, but not for words paired with meaningless squiggles, supporting the hypothesis that a testing effect requires some form of semantic content.

text.text: In other words, they report evidence against a purely visual testing effect because the testing effect was reduced/eliminated by dialing down the degree of semantic content.

Second, in work from our own lab, McCarter et al. (2025) eliminated semantics even further by pairing abstract shapes with arbitrary fill patterns, neither of which possessed obvious, universal names.
text.formatted: Second, in work from our own lab, <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">McCarter et al. (2025)</ref> eliminated semantics even further by pairing abstract shapes with arbitrary fill patterns, neither of which possessed obvious, universal names.

text.text: Like Ferreira and Wimber, we failed to find an advantage of retrieval practice, again providing evidence against a purely visual testing effect.
One concern with this study is that the visual testing effect may be small making it hard to attain statistical significance.
Arguing against this, not only did the 6 experiments of McCarter et al. repeatedly fail to find a visual testing effect, but there was also not even a non-significant trend toward one.
text.formatted: Arguing against this, not only did the 6 experiments of <ref type="bibr">McCarter et al. repeatedly</ref> fail to find a visual testing effect, but there was also not even a non-significant trend toward one.

text.text: Based on these two studies, one might conclude that a purely visual testing effect is not attainable.

However, this conclusion was recently contradicted by Li et al. (2026) who conducted a study that belongs in the third group: it employed a task design that attempts to render conceptual representations unhelpful.
text.formatted: However, this conclusion was recently contradicted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Li et al. (2026)</ref> who conducted a study that belongs in the third group: it employed a task design that attempts to render conceptual representations unhelpful.

text.text: Li et al. paired images of scenes with distinct levels of brightness/saturation and required participants to recall the brightness level when prompted with the scene image; retrieval practice improved recall of brightness, relative to restudy.

Like studies in the first group, this design paired an attribute that is purely visual (brightness) with an attribute possessing rich semantic content (a scene), so it did not remove semantic content.

However, because the attribute that had to be recalled was non-semantic (brightness) and because the task used multiple pictures corresponding to the same scene label (e.g., 12 castles, 12 bridges, etc.), it represents an attempt at the second empirical approach outlined above: eliminating the utility of conceptual labels by preventing the use of simple heuristics like "the castle was very bright".

However, the stimulus items within a category were relatively distinct, suggesting that verbal/conceptual representations could still have aided performance (e.g., "castle nestled in hills was dim, castle with rounded turrets was very bright").

Ruling out this possibility would require a manipulation of semantic content -i.e., comparison against another condition employing asemantic stimuli that are harder to verbally recode -to demonstrate that the testing effect is not weakened or eliminated when semantic content is reduced.

In the present work, we employ both empirical approaches outlined above -the explicit manipulation of semantic content by comparing meaningful to abstract stimuli, along with a task that eliminates the utility of conceptual representations.
Using this dual approach, we present the most rigorous evidence to date that an analog for the verbal memory testing effect exists for purely visual memory.
The novel task design in the current study was inspired by the repeated failure to find a testing effect in McCarter et al. (2025).
text.formatted: The novel task design in the current study was inspired by the repeated failure to find a testing effect in <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">McCarter et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: In those experiments, retrieval practice for abstract stimuli produced no advantage despite the fact that all of the experiments provided feedback during retrieval practice and the fact that 4 of the 6 experiments re-presented the whole correct object for this feedback, providing whole object visual exposure equivalent to restudy in addition to retrieval practice.
This failure to find a testing effect despite presentation of the whole object for feedback suggests that there was no learning at all from retrieval practice.

However, similar to the abstract "squiggles" condition of Ferreira and Wimber (2023), which also found no testing effect, the McCarter et al. study involved the learning of arbitrary associations between pairs of items or pairs of visual parts.
text.formatted: However, similar to the abstract "squiggles" condition of <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Ferreira and Wimber (2023)</ref>, which also found no testing effect, the McCarter et al. study involved the learning of arbitrary associations between pairs of items or pairs of visual parts.

text.text: Such arbitrary pairings are common in everyday learning and retrieval of verbal memories (such is the nature of language), and they work well for verbal memory in the lab.
Yet such arbitrary pairings are not typical of visual learning and retrieval.

The best example of visual recall in everyday situations is pattern completion in response to occluded views where a partial view of an object systematically (rather than arbitrarily) suggests the remainder of the object.

Thus, rather than arbitrary "disembodied" pairings, a more effective method for promoting visual learning -one that is natural to the visual system -may be retrieval practice in response to an occluded object cue.

We propose two highly related hypotheses: first, that a purely visual testing effect can be obtained by using a more natural form of visual retrieval practice, and second, that visual pattern completion is a domain general process that serves not only as a retrieval operation but also as a powerful learning mechanism.

These hypotheses are in line with the Primary and Convergent Retrieval (PCR) theory of Hopper and Huber (2018), an account of the testing effect which proposes that the act of retrieval induces intra-item learning, or feature-to-feature strengthening, within the target representation itself.
text.formatted: These hypotheses are in line with the Primary and Convergent Retrieval (PCR) theory of <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hopper and Huber (2018)</ref>, an account of the testing effect which proposes that the act of retrieval induces intra-item learning, or feature-to-feature strengthening, within the target representation itself.

text.text: Applied to verbal material, convergent retrieval is akin to overcoming tip-of-the-tongue -for instance, a memory cue (e.g., someone's face) can trigger partial/primary retrieval (e.g., "I think his name begins with a T") followed by full pattern completion (e.g., "Tobias"!), which promotes stronger memory for the successfully recalled verbal label.

This account therefore posits a key role for pattern completion in the testing effect: when part of a memory is provided as a cue, retrieval requires reconstructing missing features to complete the whole.
The pattern completion operation does not simply retrieve a representation -it modifies and strengthens it.
Here, we test this account for the first time in the visual domain.
We believe it is particularly applicable to the visual system because pattern completion in response to occluded views is ubiquitous in everyday situations.

This hypothesis provides a novel perspective for interpreting the prior testing effect literature: if a purely visual testing effect exists, perhaps it is easiest to demonstrate with a retrieval format more natural to the visual system, i.e., visual pattern completion induced by partial occlusion.
If correct, the hypothesis that pattern completion is a domain general learning mechanism has important implications for memory theories.
First, finding robust empirical evidence for a purely visual testing effect mediated via pattern completion would draw a clear parallel between verbal and visual mechanisms of learning and retrieval.

Second, demonstrating a benefit of retrieval practice for memory representations that are visual rather than conceptual would present a serious challenge to several influential theories of the testing effect, which claim that the effect depends on semantic mediation or pre-existing representations (Antony et al., 2017; Carpenter, 2009; Ferreira & Wimber, 2023; Pyc & Rawson, 2010; Reyna & Brainerd, 1995).
text.formatted: Second, demonstrating a benefit of retrieval practice for memory representations that are visual rather than conceptual would present a serious challenge to several influential theories of the testing effect, which claim that the effect depends on semantic mediation or pre-existing representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Antony et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Carpenter, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Ferreira & Wimber, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Pyc & Rawson, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Reyna & Brainerd, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: To ensure that we are assessing visual learning without contribution from conceptual or verbal representations, we must render any non-visual information unhelpful for solving the memory task, both during retrieval practice and at final test.

We achieve this with a novel visual occlusion retrieval task that tests memory by requiring discrimination of highly visually similar target-lure pairs that are semantically matched, such that they share conceptual and verbal representations.
As a second check on the utility of conceptual representations, in several of the experiments we manipulate the level of semantic content possessed by the stimuli.

It is impossible to eliminate semantic information entirely, but the manipulation of semantic knowledge circumvents this problem because it is attended by a clear prediction: if semantic representations contribute to the testing effect, the testing effect should be smaller when semantic information is reduced.

To demonstrate that it is part-to-whole pattern completion that is key to learning, we must compare any testing effect derived via visual occlusion retrieval practice (the novel visual occlusion retrieval task) to the testing effect obtained with whole object retrieval practice (a standard associative retrieval task).

We make this statistical comparison directly across two experiments, thereby asking if the benefits of retrieval practice occur when retrieval induces pattern completion, but not when whole object retrieval is used.
We used a novel "peephole" learning paradigm.

In this task, participants first study whole objects, then either practice retrieving the objects cued by a restricted circular aperture revealing only a fraction of the image (a "peephole") or simply restudy them via additional exposure to the whole object.
Finally, participants complete a memory test for all objects, to enable comparison of performance after retrieval practice versus additional study.

The task minimizes any utility of non-visual information by forcing performance on the final memory test to depend on finegrained discrimination of visual details: any verbal or conceptual information possessed by the target is possessed in equal measure by the foil (e.g., both target and foil are gold bells differing only in subtle visual details).
This enables measurement of an asemantic, visual testing effect.

We further probed the contribution of semantic representations to learning by manipulating the level of pre-existing semantic knowledge that the stimuli invoke; this allowed us to examine whether the size of any retrieval practice learning advantage is larger when there is greater availability of semantic representations.

Finally, we manipulated the mode of cueing memory -using as a retrieval cue either part of the item (visual occlusion) or a paired item (standard associative retrieval) -thereby promoting or eliminating part-to-whole visual pattern completion, to assess whether it is the mechanism driving retrieval-based visual learning.
General methodological details common to all studies are presented here.
In subsequent sections we present specific methodological details that pertain to each separate study.
Participants were undergraduate students from the University of Colorado Boulder who participated in the study for course credit.

Participants for all studies were recruited from the same pool of undergraduates -students enrolled in the Introduction to Psychology course at CU Boulder, participating through CU Boulder's Sona system, a cloud-based software application used to manage the research participant pool.
Specific race and gender demographic information was collected for Experiments 4, 5, 6, and 7, but not for Experiments 1, 2 and 3.

General demographic information for students enrolled in the recruitment class between 2023 and 2026 was as follows: 61% female, 39% male; 98.2% of participants aged 18-25 years, with fewer than 2% aged 26+; 4% African American, 1.5% American Indian/Alaska Native, 9.4% Asian, 14.8% Hispanic/Latino, 0.5% Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, 67% White, and 3.5% unknown.

A reasonable expectation for a testing effect study is a mean d' difference between conditions of 0.3, with a d' standard deviation of approximately 0.8.
Obtaining 80% power to detect this effect in a repeated-measures design using a two-tailed paired t-test (alpha 0.05) requires around 58 participants.
We targeted approximately this number in each study, with exact totals depending on how many participants signed up in the last 1-2 days of the experiment, through CU Boulder's Sona system.

For Experiment 7, we had many more participants for two reasons: (1) we collected fewer trials per participant resulting in a greater d' standard deviation, and (2) we ran three versions of the study that were not originally meant to be combined and were instead meant to be comparison between two halves of the experiment, but afterwards found a coding mistake in half of the experiment for the first two versions; we discarded the data from the halves with the coding mistake, and we combined the otherwise equivalent halves that suffered no error.
The experiment was coded in PsychoPy Builder and presented on a 24" computer screen with a 60-Hz refresh rate.
Data output specifications and data analysis were computed in R Studio.

text.text: For all studies that used "d-prime" (d') as the dependent variable, we calculated this measure as: d' = Z -1 (Hits) -Z -1 (FAs), where Hits = proportion of correctly-matched images correctly endorsed as intact, and False Alarms (FAs) = the proportion of mismatched images incorrectly endorsed as intact.
In this equation, Z -1 represents the inverse cumulative normal distribution function, which gives Z scores corresponding to the response rates in place of the raw response rates.
We use d' because it typically provides a more accurate measurement of memory performance than raw percentage accuracy scores, which do not take into account response bias (MacMillan, 2002).
text.formatted: We use d' because it typically provides a more accurate measurement of memory performance than raw percentage accuracy scores, which do not take into account response bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(MacMillan, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: We applied the Hautus correction to avoid infinite d' values that occur when the Hit rate equals 1 or the FA rate equals 0 (Hautus, 1995).

text.text: In the first study, we assessed whether retrieval practice produces a visual learning advantage relative to restudy when visual pattern completion is encouraged by cuing memory with a partial view.
We used 3D, photographic visual images of objects.

In everyday situations, as we move, or as objects in our visual environment move, not only do we experience occluded views of objects, we also experience un-occluded views of those same objects which provide visual feedback after the pattern completion retrieval attempt.
We mimicked this experience in our task by providing whole-object feedback after each retrieval practice test.

Such feedback is often provided in verbal testing effect paradigms and, more importantly, whole-object feedback repeatedly failed to produce a visual testing effect in the Importantly, our task used a final test format that ensured that verbal or conceptual information is unhelpful: each target was paired with a lure that possessed almost identical semantic content such that they could be discriminated only based on fine-grained visual details.

In addition, we manipulated the level of pre-existing semantic knowledge possessed by the visual stimuli, pitting nameable, meaningful objects presumed high in conceptual/semantic content against less nameable, abstract objects that are much lower in conceptual/semantic content (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: In addition, we manipulated the level of pre-existing semantic knowledge possessed by the visual stimuli, pitting nameable, meaningful objects presumed high in conceptual/semantic content against less nameable, abstract objects that are much lower in conceptual/semantic content (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: We acknowledge that no stimulus set can eliminate semantic content entirely: humans are exceptionally good at devising names or semantic interpretations for abstract images.

Instead, this manipulation of the level of conceptual content allows us to assess whether dialing up or down the engagement of pre-existing semantic representations influences the magnitude of any retrieval practice benefit (e.g., as predicted by Antony et al., 2017; Pyc & Rawson, 2010).
text.formatted: Instead, this manipulation of the level of conceptual content allows us to assess whether dialing up or down the engagement of pre-existing semantic representations influences the magnitude of any retrieval practice benefit (e.g., as predicted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Antony et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Pyc & Rawson, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: We predicted a testing effect -that is, superior memory performance following retrieval practiced than restudy -for both meaningful and abstract objects.

This is because we expect pattern completion retrieval practice to enhance memory regardless of whether the stimuli engage semantic representations or purely visual representations and, furthermore, we expect the task to minimize the utility of semantic representations.

In other words, we predicted no interaction between stimulus type (meaningful, abstract) and study condition (retrieval practice, restudy), evidencing a similar magnitude of testing effect for the two stimulus types.
We used a within-subjects design in which all participants saw two levels of stimulus type (meaningful, abstract) at three levels of Study Condition (novel, restudy, retrieval practice).
Participants first studied a series of whole object images, answering an incidental question about pleasantness to ensure attention (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Participants first studied a series of whole object images, answering an incidental question about pleasantness to ensure attention (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: Next, half of the images underwent retrieval practice, in which participants were presented with a restricted circular aperture to cue their memory of the whole item (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Next, half of the images underwent retrieval practice, in which participants were presented with a restricted circular aperture to cue their memory of the whole item (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: This design mimicked the everyday occurrence of seeing an occluded object and "filling in" missing features via part-to-whole visual pattern completion.
Our hypothesis is that such pattern completion strengthens the associations between individual features within the object (Hopper & Huber, 2018).
text.formatted: Our hypothesis is that such pattern completion strengthens the associations between individual features within the object <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hopper & Huber, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Next, to measure the efficacy of retrieval from this partial cue, participants were shown a whole object missing a circular patch in the same location used for the aperture cue (a "holepunch image", Fig. 1) and were asked if this was the correct whole object matching the aperture presented immediately prior.

Rather, this is an intact-rearranged task, requiring retrieval of missing details to confirm or reject a "match".

Sixty-three undergraduate students completed the study; seven were excluded because they failed to respond on more than 20% of trials.
Stimuli were 144 color photographs of objects.
Of these, 72 were meaningful, nameable objects, and 72 were abstract, less-nameable objects (Fig. 2).
text.formatted: Of these, 72 were meaningful, nameable objects, and 72 were abstract, less-nameable objects (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>).

text.text: Within each set of meaningful and abstract stimuli there were 12 categories of items-e.g., red lawnmowers, yellow chairs, wooden grandfather clocks-that each contained 6 highly similar exemplars (Fig. 2).
text.formatted: Within each set of meaningful and abstract stimuli there were 12 categories of items-e.g., red lawnmowers, yellow chairs, wooden grandfather clocks-that each contained 6 highly similar exemplars (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>).

text.text: These six similar exemplars were exploited in the experimental design to ensure that participants were learning and retrieving visual details, rather than relying on semantic information or verbal labels.

Specifically, the six different exemplars were divided into 3 pairs, with the two items in a pair assigned to the same study condition (restudy, retrieval practice or novel) and yoked together for the match/mismatch recognition question used at retrieval practice and final test.
For all match/mismatch tests, one stimulus in the fixed pair served as the lure when the other was the target, and vice versa.

This ensured that a target and its lure always shared the same name and similar appearance, forcing participants to remember and differentiate the specific visual features of each exemplar to respond to the memory test correctly.
Furthermore, verbal differentiation between the stimuli was made even harder by the fact that participants saw not one but six of each item type sharing the same name.

That is, if participants had been shown only two yellow chairs, they might have used a simple scheme such as "squat chair" versus "tall chair," but with six stimuli sharing the same name, easy verbal differentiation between all stimuli was precluded.

Finally, because all stimuli were studied an equal number of times, and all target-lure stimulus pairs were assigned to the same study condition (either retrieval practice, restudy or novel), targets and lures were matched for familiarity, forcing memory performance to rely on recall of missing visual details.
For the images of meaningful objects, many were taken from the databases of Konkle and Oliva (2012).

text.text: However, when using these stimulus databases, we took only one exemplar for a particular category from the database (e.g., one red lawnmower) and found 5 other similar exemplars from other sources.
After selecting the first image in each category, the 5 additional image exemplars were derived using Google Reverse Image Search or created via an online morphing application (3DThis.com).

All images of objects were set on a square white background and scaled to be of similar size within the square. one category of abstract stimulus -orange widgets -again grouped into 3 maximally visually similar pairs.
For each stimulus, an "aperture" and a complementary "holepunch" image were created (e.g., Fig 1., middle top panel).
text.formatted: For each stimulus, an "aperture" and a complementary "holepunch" image were created (e.g., Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>., middle top panel).

text.text: Aperture size was consistent across all stimuli.

Aperture location varied from one stimulus category to the next (e.g., chair, bell, car, etc.) and was chosen manually so that the aperture for every stimulus provided a somewhat plausible "match" to the "holepunch" of the lure stimulus with which it was paired.
This was done under the constraint that aperture location was identical across all 6 exemplars for a given stimulus category.
The experiment was divided into 6 blocks; the first block contained only a study/learning phase, whereas the remaining 5 blocks contained a study/learning phase and a final test phase.

This is because the blocks were interleaved, such that the study and additional learning phases (i.e., restudy and retrieval practice) for a particular set of images (e.g., red lawnmowers, yellow chairs, orange widgets, and red squiggly sculptures) were followed by the final test phase for the images learned in the preceding block (e.g., blue cars, white bathtubs, black-and-white squiggles, and black cylinders).
Interleaving in this manner allowed for a delay and "context change"
between study/learning and final test for each set of images (Jang & Huber, 2008), which is known to be important for promoting a robust testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006).
text.formatted: between study/learning and final test for each set of images <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Jang & Huber, 2008)</ref>, which is known to be important for promoting a robust testing effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Roediger & Karpicke, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, the first block consisted only of study and additional learning (no final test) of the first set of images.
In the second block, participants first completed study and additional learning for the second set of images, followed by final test on the images studied in the first block.
The third block began with study and additional learning for the third set of images, followed by a final test for the images studied in the second block, and so on.
The 6 exemplars within each item category were grouped into 3 pairs based on similarity (Fig. 2).
text.formatted: The 6 exemplars within each item category were grouped into 3 pairs based on similarity (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>).

text.text: One stimulus pair in each category was designated to be restudied, another to undergo retrieval practice, and the third to fulfill the novel condition at final test.
The assignment of specific exemplar pairs to study conditions was randomly counterbalanced across participants.

At the start of each block, participants studied 16 whole items, which were drawn from two meaningful categories (e.g., red lawnmowers, yellow chairs) and two abstract categories (e.g., orange widgets, red squiggly sculptures), with 4 exemplars of each.
The 4 exemplars for each category corresponded to the "restudy" pair and the "retrieval practice" pair from each category; the "novel" pair for each category did not appear in the study phase.
Thus, the study block comprised 8 meaningful objects (2 restudy pairs, 2 retrieval practice pairs) and 8 abstract objects.

In the initial study phase, item category exemplars were presented sequentially, grouped by category, to make it clear that the participant was viewing 4 similar but distinct exemplars (e.g., 4 red lawnmowers).
Each image was presented for 3 seconds along with a prompt to rate the pleasantness of the image from 1 to 3, followed by a blank screen for 1 second.
After initial study of all 16 studied items in the block, participants engaged in two rounds of "additional learning" for all studied items.
Additional learning comprised 2 rounds of restudy and 2 rounds of retrieval practice, interleaved.
Whether the sequence began with restudy or retrieval practice was counterbalanced across participants, with the same order being used for all blocks for a given participant.

In each round of restudy, 8 of the original 16 whole images (4 meaningful and 4 abstract; those designated as "restudy" pairs) were presented once each, this time in random order, again for 3 seconds with the same pleasantness rating followed by a 1 second blank.
In each retrieval practice round, the remaining 8 images (4 meaningful and 4 abstract; those designated as "retrieval practice" pairs) underwent a practice retrieval test (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: In each retrieval practice round, the remaining 8 images (4 meaningful and 4 abstract; those designated as "retrieval practice" pairs) underwent a practice retrieval test (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: For this, a small circular aperture of one of the images was first presented for 3 seconds, and the participant was asked how well they could remember the whole image that went with that part, rating their memory from 1 to 3, followed by a 1 second blank.
Next, participants viewed a whole image missing the circular aperture; this was either the correct whole image (matched), or the other image in the stimulus pair (mismatched).
Participants viewed this "holepunch" image for 3 seconds and were asked if this was the correct whole image that matched the aperture (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Participants viewed this "holepunch" image for 3 seconds and were asked if this was the correct whole image that matched the aperture (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: Finally, after another blank screen of 1 second, feedback was provided by showing the correct whole image for 1 second, with text informing the participant whether their response was correct or incorrect.

Across the two rounds of practice test for each image, one trial was matched (test probe was a holepunch image for the same stimulus as the aperture) and the other was mismatched (test probe was a holepunch image for the other image in the stimulus pair).
Lastly, each block (except the first block) included a set of 24 final test trials.

Here, all 6 image exemplars from all 4 studied categories were tested: in each category, 4 of these exemplars had been encountered during study and additional learning (2 restudy, 2 retrieval practice), and 2 were novel, providing a baseline for how well participants could discern the correct pairing without learning.
At final test, whether the image was correctly paired or mismatched was randomized to have half matched and half mismatched.
No feedback was provided at final test.

Before beginning the experiment, all participants saw a preview of the task, including examples of an initial study trial, a restudy trial, a retrieval practice trial, and a final test trial, using a single meaningful object that was not seen later in the experiment.
We measured performance on the final test -an intact-rearranged recognition task -with signal detection theory, which yields d' scores.

This measure corrects for changes in response bias (e.g., the tendency to endorse an item as "old", regardless of memory strength), yielding an unbiased measure of memory discrimination ability (MacMillan, 2002).
text.formatted: This measure corrects for changes in response bias (e.g., the tendency to endorse an item as "old", regardless of memory strength), yielding an unbiased measure of memory discrimination ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(MacMillan, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: As seen in Fig. 3, there was a memory performance advantage for retrieval practice over restudy -a testing effect -for both meaningful and abstract objects.
text.formatted: As seen in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>, there was a memory performance advantage for retrieval practice over restudy -a testing effect -for both meaningful and abstract objects.

text.text: Numerical summary statistics for all experiments, including hit and false alarm rates, are provided in the Supplementary Materials.
Error bars are +/-standard error of the mean across participants.
For both stimulus sets there was a significant benefit of retrieval practice relative to restudy for performance at final test.
To assess d', we conducted a two-way [3x2] repeated-measures ANOVA with two withinsubjects factors: Study Condition (novel, restudy, retrieval practice) and Stimulus Type (meaningful, abstract).

This revealed a main effect of Study Condition, F(2,110) = 23.10, p < .001, η²p = .296, and a main effect of Stimulus Type, F(1,55) = 19.41, p < 0.001, η²p = .261, but no significant interaction between Study Condition and Stimulus Type, F(2,110) = 1.17, p = 0.31.

text.text: To investigate what drove the main effect of Study Condition, we conducted planned comparisons via paired-samples t-tests; these indicated a significant difference between restudy and retrieval practice, t(55) = -4.49, p < 0.001, dz = -0.60, in which the mean d' was higher for retrieval practice (M = 1.98, SD = 0.65) than for restudy (M = 1.63, SD = 0.65), a significant difference between retrieval practice and novel, t(55) = 7.48, p < 0.001, dz = 1.00, in which the mean d' was higher for retrieval practice than for novel (M = 1.43, SD = 0.55), and a significant difference between restudy and novel, t(55) = 2.11, p = 0.040, dz = 0.28, in which the mean d' was higher for restudy than for novel.

text.text: In this novel visual recall paradigm, performance after both restudy and retrieval practice exceeded that in the novel condition, indicating that learning occurred.

More importantly, retrieval practice produced better performance than restudy, providing the most robust evidence to date for a visual testing effect that does not rely on verbal recoding of visual images.
Specifically, because the final test eliminated the utility of verbal labels, the observed retrieval practice advantage must depend on visual representations.
Furthermore, manipulating the level of semantic content did not influence the size of the testing effect: there was no interaction between Study Condition and Stimulus Type.

In fact, the magnitude of the retrieval practice advantage was numerically greater for thee abstract items, which were less nameable and less likely to engage semantic representations than the meaningful items.

Any theory claiming that semantic representations are key to reaping the benefits of retrieval practice would predict that the testing effect should be reduced when semantic content is reduced (i.e., in abstract relative to meaningful objects).

Thus, these findings contradict prominent theories of the testing effect, such as those suggesting that it depends on semantic mediation (Carpenter, 2009; Pyc & Rawson, 2010) or on well-established, pre-existing cortical representations (Antony et al., 2017; Ferreira & Wimber, 2023).
text.formatted: Thus, these findings contradict prominent theories of the testing effect, such as those suggesting that it depends on semantic mediation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Carpenter, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Pyc & Rawson, 2010)</ref> or on well-established, pre-existing cortical representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Antony et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Ferreira & Wimber, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The main effect of stimulus type should not be interpreted as carrying any theoretical significance.
As in all recognition memory paradigms, general performance levels in this task are driven largely by the similarity of the targets and the lures.
Each target was yoked with a lure, so the greater the similarity of these target-lure pairs, the poorer the performance.
This main effect suggests only that we did not fully equate target-lure similarity for meaningful versus abstract items.

However, it was not necessary to do so: our goal was to look for a testing effect, i.e., better performance after Retrieval Practice than after Restudy, and this effect does not depend on overall, mean performance levels collapsed across Study Conditions, as long as they are neither at ceiling nor at floor (which they were not).

In sum, the success of this visual occlusion paradigm in eliciting a testing effect suggests that part-to-whole learning of the visual representation may be the mechanism behind the retrieval practice advantage.
We test this claim directly in Experiment 2.

To investigate whether the key advantage of retrieval practice is driven by part-to-whole pattern completion, in Experiment 2 we removed visual occlusion, instead using arbitrary cuetarget pairings as is customary in the verbal testing effect literature and as was the case in prior failures to find a purely visual testing effect (Ferreira & Wimber, 2023; McCarter et al., 2025).
text.formatted: To investigate whether the key advantage of retrieval practice is driven by part-to-whole pattern completion, in Experiment 2 we removed visual occlusion, instead using arbitrary cuetarget pairings as is customary in the verbal testing effect literature and as was the case in prior failures to find a purely visual testing effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Ferreira & Wimber, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">McCarter et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Critically, Experiment 2 used the same visual objects as Experiment 1, with the same target-lure pairings that enforced memory decisions based on visual details.

In this experiment, each image was paired with a word at study, and the word was used as a retrieval cue at test, such that participants no longer engaged in part-to-whole pattern completion (Fig. 4).
text.formatted: In this experiment, each image was paired with a word at study, and the word was used as a retrieval cue at test, such that participants no longer engaged in part-to-whole pattern completion (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>).

text.text: Instead, correct memory decisions relied upon an arbitrary association formed at study between the image and the word.
This was a very difficult word-image association task because participants associated 6 different words with each of 6 highly similar items within a category (e.g., 6 red lawnmowers).

Crucially, during retrieval practice, to give the correct answer from the word cue, participants could not exploit verbal/semantic associations, because the 6 distinct target images shared a verbal label, e.g., lawnmower.
Instead, they needed to remember specific visual details -this red lawnmower and not that red lawnmower.

We propose that the generation of fine-grained visual detail proceeds via part-to-part pattern completion; but we expected this visual pattern completion to be very difficult without starting from a partially occluded cue.

Hence, we predicted retrieval practice in this task to produce limited learning, which should be equaled or exceeded by the learning from restudy (in which the visual details are provided), eliminating the testing effect for both classes of visual object.

Stimuli were the same images of meaningful and abstract objects from Experiment 1.
However, in this study, no apertures nor holepunch images were used, only whole images, and each image was randomly paired with an unrelated word, presented at the top of the screen (Fig. 4).

text.text: In addition, a given participant saw only 4 of the 6 images in each category (e.g., 4 of the 6 lawnmowers) because the novel condition was not included.

The novel condition was dropped because participants could not possibly know the correct response to an arbitrary word cue for a cue-target pairing that was never studied (i.e., the novel condition would necessarily have an average d' of 0).
Words were selected from The Glasgow Norms to be primarily nouns with a length of 4 to 7 letters, a rating of 5 in concreteness, high imageability, and high familiarity (Scott et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Words were selected from The Glasgow Norms to be primarily nouns with a length of 4 to 7 letters, a rating of 5 in concreteness, high imageability, and high familiarity <ref type="bibr">(Scott et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The procedure was the same as for Experiment 1, again using within-subjects factors Stimulus Type and Study Condition, with the following three modifications.

First, the stimuli presented for initial study (and restudy) were whole images paired with words, and the participant was asked to rate how easy or difficult it was to pair the image with that word (Fig. 4).
text.formatted: First, the stimuli presented for initial study (and restudy) were whole images paired with words, and the participant was asked to rate how easy or difficult it was to pair the image with that word (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>).

text.text: Second, for retrieval practice and final test, instead of cuing memory with an aperture, participants were cued with a word and asked how well they could remember the image that was paired with that word, rating their memory from 1 to 3.

The match/mismatch test probe was a whole image that was either the correct image that had been paired with that word at study, or the other image from the pre-assigned stimulus pair (i.e., the same stimulus pair system used in Experiment 1, see Figs. 1 and 4).
text.formatted: The match/mismatch test probe was a whole image that was either the correct image that had been paired with that word at study, or the other image from the pre-assigned stimulus pair (i.e., the same stimulus pair system used in Experiment 1, see Figs. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>).

text.text: Retrieval practice trials included feedback as in Experiment 1, i.e., the whole correct image was shown for 1 sec along with text indicating the correctness of the response.
Third, final test no longer included novel items, because novel items in this paradigm are never seen at initial study, therefore there can be no correct answer as to what image goes with the word.
All block lengths, timing, and counterbalancing were identical to Experiment 1.
Performance on intact-rearranged image-word recognition is shown in Fig. 5.
text.formatted: Performance on intact-rearranged image-word recognition is shown in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">5</ref>.

text.text: In this task there is no novel condition because the pairing of a word and image is arbitrary, and so it could not be known which image to retrieve in the absence of learning.
A two-way [2x2] repeatedmeasures ANOVA revealed no significant interaction between Study Condition (restudy, retrieval practice] and Stimulus Type (meaningful, abstract), F(1,59) = 1.11, p = 0.30.
We also found no main effect of Study Condition on d', F(1,59) = 1.28, p = 0.26, but a main effect of Stimulus Type, F(1,59) = 19.84, p < 0.001, η²p = .252.
text.formatted: We also found no main effect of Study Condition on d', F(1,59) = 1.28, p = 0.26, but a main effect of Stimulus Type, F(1,59) = 19.84, p < 0.001, η²p = .252.

text.text: Given that we included only retrieval practice and restudy conditions (no novel condition), the lack of an effect of Study Condition means that we found no evidence for a testing effect.

Visual inspection of the means and error bars for all Stimulus Types and Study Conditions (Fig. 5) makes it clear that memory performance is well above chance (all d' values substantially greater than zero).
text.formatted: Visual inspection of the means and error bars for all Stimulus Types and Study Conditions (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">5</ref>) makes it clear that memory performance is well above chance (all d' values substantially greater than zero).

text.text: Hence, the lack of evidence for a testing effect cannot be attributed to an absence of learning in general.

There is no novel condition -i.e., intact/rearranged judgement for items that have never been studied nor practicedbecause the pairing of a word with an image is arbitrary and so d' in the novel condition would necessarily be 0.
In this paradigm, although both retrieval practice and restudy were both above 0, there was no advantage of retrieval practice over restudy for either stimulus set.
With visual occlusion and the concomitant part-to-whole pattern completion removed, we found no significant testing effect for meaningful nor for abstract objects.
Without the aperture cue and the intra-item learning that putatively occurs when "filling in" of the rest of the image, there was no learning benefit to retrieval.

In this paradigm, instead of part-to-whole pattern completion, participants were cued via an arbitrary association from a previously paired word to the object, which did not produce a learning benefit.

This replicates previous findings of no testing effect for a fine-grained visual discrimination task when retrieval depends on the association with an arbitrary memory cue (Ferreira & Wimber, 2023; McCarter et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This replicates previous findings of no testing effect for a fine-grained visual discrimination task when retrieval depends on the association with an arbitrary memory cue <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Ferreira & Wimber, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">McCarter et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The contrast between Experiments 1 and 2 suggests that the lack of a visual testing effect in these prior studies reflected visual retrieval practice that failed to encourage the kind of part-to-part learning induced by visual occlusion, combined with a final retrieval test that nevertheless required memory for the visual details of the objects.
A central prediction of our account is that visual pattern completion is the mechanism that drives learning.

Experiment 1 encouraged participants to retrieve whole objects from an occluded view, which we hypothesize induces pattern completion, whereas Experiment 2 eliminated the opportunity for part-to-whole learning because it did not use occluded views to cue retrieval.
If visual pattern completion is driving the testing effect, then the retrieval-practice advantage should be larger in Experiment 1 than in Experiment 2.

This prediction cannot be tested by simply noting that the testing effect is statistically significant in one experiment but not in another; instead, we must directly test whether the retrieval-practice advantage differed in magnitude across task types (Nieuwenhuis et al., 2011).
text.formatted: This prediction cannot be tested by simply noting that the testing effect is statistically significant in one experiment but not in another; instead, we must directly test whether the retrieval-practice advantage differed in magnitude across task types <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Nieuwenhuis et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, we conducted a 2 × 2 mixed between-within ANOVA on d′ scores collapsed across Stimulus Type, with Study Condition (restudy and retrieval practice only; we excluded novel from Experiment 1 because it did not exist for Experiment 2) as a within-subjects factor and Task Type (Experiment 1, Experiment 2) as a between-subjects factor.
There was a significant interaction between Study Condition (restudy, retrieval practice) and Task (Experiment 1, Experiment 2), F(1,114) = 5.48, p = 0.021, η²p = .046.
We also found a main effect of Study Condition on d', F(1,114) = 15.62, p < 0.001, η²p = .120, and a main effect of Task, F(1,114) = 7.42, p = 0.0074, η²p = .061.
text.formatted: We also found a main effect of Study Condition on d', F(1,114) = 15.62, p < 0.001, η²p = .120, and a main effect of Task, F(1,114) = 7.42, p = 0.0074, η²p = .061.

text.text: Thus, the testing effect was larger when occlusion-based learning was employed (Experiment 1) than when it was not (Experiment 2), suggesting that pattern completion is a crucial driver of retrieval-induced learning.
In Experiment 1, the abstract, less meaningful stimuli were 3-dimensional color photographs, and some possessed passing resemblances to meaningful objects.

Furthermore, they possessed coherent global form, which is likely to engage visual regions beyond striate cortex such as lateral occipital cortex (Kourtzi & Kanwisher, 2001; Malach et al., 1995) and thus perhaps these stimuli draw on pre-existing object knowledge.
text.formatted: Furthermore, they possessed coherent global form, which is likely to engage visual regions beyond striate cortex such as lateral occipital cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kourtzi & Kanwisher, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Malach et al., 1995)</ref> and thus perhaps these stimuli draw on pre-existing object knowledge.

text.text: In order to further reduce any engagement of pre-existing object representations or semantic knowledge, we replicated Experiment 1 but replaced the 3-dimensional abstract objects with Mandarin Chinese characters, testing only participants unfamiliar with the Mandarin language for whom these stimuli constitute meaningless 2-dimensional symbols (Fig. 6).
text.formatted: In order to further reduce any engagement of pre-existing object representations or semantic knowledge, we replicated Experiment 1 but replaced the 3-dimensional abstract objects with Mandarin Chinese characters, testing only participants unfamiliar with the Mandarin language for whom these stimuli constitute meaningless 2-dimensional symbols (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">6</ref>).

text.text: We employed the same task procedure as in Experiment 1 (Fig. 7), predicting that intra-item learning would again occur during retrieval practice, leading to a visual testing effect for Mandarin characters.
text.formatted: We employed the same task procedure as in Experiment 1 (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">7</ref>), predicting that intra-item learning would again occur during retrieval practice, leading to a visual testing effect for Mandarin characters.

text.text: Because final test format eliminates the utility of verbal/conceptual representations by requiring fine-grained visual discrimination, we expected learning to be supported by visual rather than semantic representations; we therefore predicted that the testing effect would be at least as large for Mandarin symbols as for meaningful objects.
Sixty-eight undergraduate students completed the experiment; 6 were excluded because they failed to respond on more than 20% of trials.
Stimuli were the same 72 images of meaningful objects as Experiment 1, but the abstract objects were now replaced with 72 Mandarin Chinese characters.

These characters were taken from a list of characters taught to first graders learning to read and write Mandarin and were grouped into categories containing 6 exemplars based on visual similarity to a Mandarin nonreader (Fig. 6). organized into categories by visual similarity from the perspective of a non-Mandarin reader, disregarding their meaning in Mandarin.

Procedure was the same as for Experiment 1, with the following modifications.
First, the abstract objects were replaced with Mandarin Chinese characters.
Second, given the increased difficulty of learning Mandarin characters for non-Mandarin readers, the number of unique stimuli per block was reduced.

Specifically, rather than 16 studied items, there were only 8 studied items, comprising 4 items from a single meaningful object category, e.g., clocks, and 4 characters from a single Mandarin category based on visual similarity (see Supplemental Materials).

Thus, only one meaningful category (4 items) and one Chinese character category (4 items) were learned per block; 2 of the meaningful items were assigned to "restudy" and 2 to "retrieval practice," and the same for abstract items.
Second, we increased the number of rounds of additional learning from 2 to 3.

Third, to ensure that there were enough final test trials to accurately assess memory performance, the number of final test trials per item was doubled (achieved via each item being tested twice, once in an "intact" trial and once in a "rearranged" trial).

Fourth, we increased the total number of final test blocks from 5 to 8 (now, there were 9 blocks in total, of which 8 included a final test because, as in Experiment 1, the first block did not include final test).
Memory was again measured with d' (Fig. 8).

text.text: Memory performance for Experiment 3.
Individual dots show d' values for individual participants; black markers show group mean d' for each condition.
Error bars are +/-standard error of the mean across participants.
As in Experiment 1, there was a significant advantage of retrieval practice over restudy for both stimulus types.
As in Experiment 1, we found a testing effect for both meaningful and abstract (here, Mandarin) stimuli, and no significant interaction between Stimulus Type and Study Condition.
Task performance for Mandarin characters overall was worse than for meaningful objects (a main effect of Stimulus Type with lower d' for Mandarin stimuli), including for novel items.

This main effect merely indicates that for the abstract stimuli of Experiment 3, we used target-lure pairings that were more similar (i.e., difficult to discriminate) than the target-lure pairings of meaningful objects.

Of note, this main effect was in the opposite direction compared to Experiment 1, demonstrating a robust visual testing effect for abstract objects regardless of whether the visual discrimination task is a little more difficult (Exp 3) or a little easier (Exp 1) for the abstract items.

In any case, the important learning result is indexed by the difference between study conditions, and within the Mandarin character stimulus set, the same pattern emerged across novel, restudy, and retrieval practice conditions, namely, a robust testing effect.

The absence of an interaction suggests that the magnitude of the testing effect is similar in size regardless of whether the stimuli engage high-level, well-established visual object representations that contain semantic information, or low-level representations of 2-dimensional black-and-white visual symbols.

This finding further challenges theories that claim the testing effect depends on pre-existing cortical representations (Antony et al., 2017; Ferreira & Wimber, 2023) and suggests a strong parallel between the mechanisms by which retrieval practice enhances learning for verbalizable, conceptually meaningful materials and modality-specific visual information.
text.formatted: This finding further challenges theories that claim the testing effect depends on pre-existing cortical representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Antony et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Ferreira & Wimber, 2023)</ref> and suggests a strong parallel between the mechanisms by which retrieval practice enhances learning for verbalizable, conceptually meaningful materials and modality-specific visual information.

text.text: In Experiments 1 and 3, we found a robust visual testing effect when memory at final test was probed with the same cue that had been presented for retrieval practice.
This demonstrates that the specific association from the part used as a cue to the remainder of the image was strengthened by repeated retrieval via that association.
We hypothesize that this advantage emerges because the partial cue triggers pattern completion, which induces part-to-part learning.

However, it is unclear whether the enhancement applies only when cuing retrieval on the final test with that specific practiced part of the whole image, or whether one could cue retrieval with a different image part at final test and observe the same benefit of retrieval practice.

The model of Hopper and Huber (2018), in which retrieval strengthens the intra-item associations between individual features of a memory representation, predicts that the learning underlying the testing effect is directional; this is because it depends on the temporal order in which features are "completed," in line with the timing constraints of synaptic learning rules (Aenugu & Huber, 2021).
text.formatted: The model of <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hopper and Huber (2018)</ref>, in which retrieval strengthens the intra-item associations between individual features of a memory representation, predicts that the learning underlying the testing effect is directional; this is because it depends on the temporal order in which features are "completed," in line with the timing constraints of synaptic learning rules <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aenugu & Huber, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: That is, if pattern completion unfolds from feature A to feature B, then the later ability to retrieve feature B when cued with feature A will be enhanced more than the ability to retrieve feature A when cued with feature B. Under this account, the learning benefit of retrieval practice should preferentially apply to the cue used at practice, with less transfer if a novel cue is used at test, because the novel cue will cause features to be completed in a different order. Hopper & Huber (2018) confirmed this prediction in a recall paradigm with word stimuli.

text.text: In the present visual memory task, we predicted that the part-to-whole links that are learned would be cuedependent, such that changing the location of the aperture from practice to final test should reduce or eliminate the testing effect.
In Experiment 4, we tested this prediction.
Fifty-eight undergraduate students completed the study; 6 were excluded because they failed to respond on more than 20% of trials.

Thirty-two of the participants were female, 26 were male; 6 were Hispanic/Latine and 52 not Hispanic/Latino; 1 participant was American Indian/Alaskan Native, 8 Asian, 1 African American, 1 Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, 46
White, and 1 chose not to answer.
Stimuli were the same meaningful and abstract stimuli as in Experiment 1 but with multiple novel locations for the circular aperture cues and corresponding holepunch images.

Specifically, each object in the retrieval practice condition was now associated with 4 distinct aperture views of the object; these were used once each across the 3 practice rounds and the final test (Fig. 9).

text.text: At each test (whether retrieval practice or final), the "holepunch" image used to probe memory with a match/mismatch judgment had a circular piece missing at the location corresponding to the aperture just used as a cue.
The procedure followed that of Experiment 3 in terms of the number and type of items per block and total number of blocks, but there were two changes from Experiment 3.
First, abstract 3D objects (from Experiment 1) were used instead of Mandarin characters.
Second, the apertures used to cue memory were drawn from a different location on the object for each round of retrieval practice and for final test (Fig. 9).
