text.text: As predicted, both restudy and retrieval practice yielded learning compared to novel (unstudied) items, but there was no testing effect, i.e., no reliable difference between restudy and retrieval practice.
That is, we failed to find any transfer of learning from retrieval practice when retrieval practice entailed a different aperture than the final test.

This suggests that the retrieval induced learning seen in Experiments 1 and 3 is specific, applying only to the association between the aperture used in retrieval practice and the remainder of the image, and not to associations between other, unpracticed parts of the image.

This aligns with the prediction of Hopper & Huber (2018) that practicing recall with a specific cue should strengthen associations from that cue to other features of the memory, but not associations from other unpracticed cues.
text.formatted: This aligns with the prediction of <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hopper & Huber (2018)</ref> that practicing recall with a specific cue should strengthen associations from that cue to other features of the memory, but not associations from other unpracticed cues.

text.text: Applied to everyday visual occlusion, this suggests how the learning benefits of visual occlusion for real-world object representations accrue: as an observer moves relative to a 3D object, they encounter repeated experiences of occlusion of the same object from different viewpoints, providing distinct learning experiences that strengthen different part-to-part associations to build a robust whole object representation.

Experiment 4 demonstrated that the learning benefits in this novel paradigm are specific to the learned retrieval cue, and this lack of generalization was predicted by a computational model of the testing effect (Aenugu & Huber, 2021).
text.formatted: Experiment 4 demonstrated that the learning benefits in this novel paradigm are specific to the learned retrieval cue, and this lack of generalization was predicted by a computational model of the testing effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aenugu & Huber, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, it is important to establish whether this learning enhances retrieval of the whole from the part, in which case it should generalize to other types of memory responses when using the same aperture cue, or whether the learning concerns narrow task demands about which object to choose from among two specific similar objects.
In other words, is the learning from part to whole or from part to yes/no matching decision?

An absence of generalization to other test formats might suggest that the learning advantage accrues to idiosyncratic properties of the task rather than reflecting increased robustness of the visual object representations in memory.
To examine the generalizability of the observed visual testing effect, in Experiment 5 we replicated Experiment 1 but with a different test format at final test than during retrieval practice.

If performance on this task is still enhanced by retrieval practice, this suggests that learning produces a more robust representation of the object-one that can be flexibly used to provide information that aids performance in different retrieval formats.
Sixty-seven undergraduate students completed the study; 4 were excluded because they failed to respond on more than 20% of trials.
Thirty-nine of the participants were female, 28 were male; 5 Hispanic/Latino, 59 not Hispanic/Latino; 1 American Indian/Alaskan Native, 9
Asian, 2 African American, 1 Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, 54 White.
Stimuli were the same meaningful and abstract objects as in Experiment 1.
At final test, participants were first shown an aperture and asked how well they remembered the whole image it came from (not shown here, see Fig. 2).
text.formatted: At final test, participants were first shown an aperture and asked how well they remembered the whole image it came from (not shown here, see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>).

text.text: Next, the aperture disappeared from view and participants were immediately shown an array containing all six exemplars from that stimulus group (e.g., "red lawnmowers"), each with a patch corresponding to the location of the just-seen aperture removed from the image (i.e., "holepunch" images).
Participants were prompted to select the lawnmower from which they believed the just-seen aperture had been drawn.
The procedure followed that of Experiment 3 in terms of the number and type of items per block and total number of blocks.
However, there were two key differences.
First, abstract objects were used instead of Mandarin characters (i.e., the same stimuli as Experiment 1).
Second, at final test, instead of the single match/mismatch probe, participants were presented with an aperture followed by a 6-alternative forced choice (6-AFC) recognition task (Fig. 11).
text.formatted: Second, at final test, instead of the single match/mismatch probe, participants were presented with an aperture followed by a 6-alternative forced choice (6-AFC) recognition task (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">11</ref>).

text.text: The 6 items in the array were the holepunch images corresponding to all 6 stimuli in the category from which the aperture cue was drawn (e.g., if the aperture cue was from a red lawnmower, the holepunch images from all 6 red lawnmowers were shown in the 6-AFC array).
One of the 6 "holepunch" items in the test array was the item that matched the aperture, and this had to be selected for a correct response.

text.text: Next, to investigate the nature of the interaction between Study Condition and Stimulus Type, i.e., to determine whether the testing effect itself differed by stimulus type, we compared the magnitude of the difference between restudy and retrieval practice for the two stimulus types; this was significant, t(62) = 2.76, p = 0.0077, dz = 0.347, with the mean difference being higher for abstract objects (M = 0.073, SD = 0.12) than for meaningful objects (M = 0.012, SD = 0.12).

Finally, given the interaction, we also conducted post hoc comparisons via paired-sample t-tests for each Stimulus Type separately; these indicated no significant difference between retrieval practice and restudy for meaningful, t(62) = -0.76, p = 0.45, but a significant difference between these conditions for abstract, t(62) = -4.65, p < 0.001, dz = 0.586.

text.text: As in Experiments 1 and 3, we found a testing effect in which retrieval practice elicited better final memory test performance than restudy, although here it was driven primarily by abstract rather than meaningful objects.
Nonetheless, a testing effect was still obtained even though the format of the final test differed substantially from the format used for retrieval practice.
This contrasts with Experiment 4, in which we did not obtain a testing effect because learning apparently did not generalize from one aperture to another.

Thus, while practice at retrieving the whole image from one specific aperture cue does not transfer to other aperture cues, the learning advantage of retrieval practice for the practiced cue nonetheless generalizes to retrieval in other settings, e.g., a 6AFC test, at least for abstract objects.

This suggests that partto-whole pattern completion benefits learning by increasing the robustness of learned visual representations, specifically, the strength of the association between the features of the practiced cue and the features of the whole image.
It is interesting that the testing effect was significantly larger for abstract than meaningful items -in fact, there was a testing effect for the former but not the latter.

This aligns with the suggestion that retrieval practice increases the robustness of learned visual representations, because it is with abstract objects, which are less familiar to the observer, that there is more to learn (i.e., the representational strength is further from ceiling, allowing a benefit to emerge).
We further discuss this difference between abstract and meaningful objects in the General Discussion.

In Experiments 1 through 5, whenever we employed a visual occlusion-based cuing procedure using the same cue for retrieval practice and final test, retrieval practice elicited better performance at final test than restudy.
However, these experiments assigned stimulus items to study conditions in a manner that may have produced an interference-related disadvantage for restudied items.

Specifically, there were 6 distinct exemplars for each stimulus category (e.g., 6 lawnmowers, 6 chairs, 6 exemplars for each category of abstract item, etc.) of which 2 were always assigned to retrieval practice, 2 to restudy and 2 to novel.

Thus, the same two specific lawnmowers were always assigned to retrieval practice for a given participant, such that only those two lawnmower apertures and "holepunch" probe images were seen prior to final test, with the apertures and holepunch images of the two restudy lawnmowers never seen until final test.

In light of this "within-category" manipulation of retrieval practice and restudy, it is possible that, at final test, attempts to retrieve the correct item for apertures in the restudy condition were subject to interference from the better-learned apertures and holepunch probes for retrieval practiced items.

In Experiment 6, to rule out this possibility and demonstrate that the superior memory performance for retrieval practiced items is driven by enhanced learning, we modified the assignment of stimulus categories to study conditions.

Here, distinct object categories were assigned to each study condition (i.e., a "between-category" manipulation), so that all 6 items from one category (e.g., lawnmowers) were assigned to the same study condition (e.g., restudy) and all 6 items from a different category (e.g., chairs) were assigned to a separate study condition (e.g., retrieval practice).

If retrieval practiced items still elicit better performance at final test than restudied items, this would demonstrate that the testing effect is not driven by depressed performance in the restudy condition due to interference from highly similar apertures and holepunch probe images (from the same category) that were learned via retrieval practice.
Sixty-Two undergraduate students completed the study; 10 were excluded because they failed to respond on more than 20% of trials.
Forty-seven of the participants were female, 14 male, 1 chose not to answer.
Fifteen of the participants were Hispanic/Latino, 44 not Hispanic/Latino; 4 were American Indian/Alaskan Native, 5 Asian, 50 White, and 3 chose not to answer.
Stimuli were the same meaningful and abstract objects as in Experiment 1.
The procedure was the same as Experiment 3 in terms of number of items per block and number of blocks.
However, abstract objects (from Experiment 1) were used instead of Mandarin characters, and the assignment of stimuli to study conditions was different from Experiment 3.

Specifically, distinct object categories were assigned to each study condition, so that all 6 items from one category (e.g., red lawnmowers) were assigned to the same study condition (either restudy, retrieval practice, or novel).

Each block still contained 2 restudied stimuli, 2 retrieval practiced stimuli and 2 novel stimuli from each of the meaningful and abstract stimulus sets, yielding 8 items for study and 12 items at final test.
There were again 9 blocks in total, with 8 blocks that contained a final test phase.

But this time, if lawnmowers were designated as "restudied" then one pair of lawnmowers would appear for restudy in each of 3 different blocks; if yellow chairs were designated as "retrieval practiced" then one pair of yellow chairs would be presented for retrieval practice in each of 3 different blocks, and so on.

This scheme entailed that 2 items from each of 3 categories (novel, restudy and retrieval practice) were never given a final test, because there was no final test for items studied in the last block, as in previous experiments.

The assignment of specific categories to study conditions was counterbalanced across participants, to mitigate against any biasing effect of inherent stimulus properties that were not fully balanced within a participant.

text.text: Thus, both stimulus types exhibited a testing effect.

These data indicate that relatively worse performance in the restudy conditions of Experiments 1, 3, and 5 was not driven by within-category interference from the highly familiar apertures and hole punch images assigned to the retrieval practice condition.

In Experiment 6, we assigned distinct stimulus categories to the separate study conditions, such that no aperture from the retrieval practice condition was similar to any aperture from the restudy condition, and yet we still obtained a robust retrieval practice advantage.
In fact, the testing effect magnitude was numerically larger with this modified stimulus assignment.
Experiment 2 differed from Experiments 1, 3, 5 and 6 in that it did not find an advantage for retrieval-practiced items.

However, in Experiment 2, there was one important difference that may have given restudied items a boost not present in the other experiments: restudied items were shown alongside their separately presented retrieval cue (the paired word), drawing attention to the cue.
This may have provided optimal conditions for strengthening the association between the cue and target image during restudy.

In contrast, in Experiments 1, 3, 5 and 6, although restudied items contained the retrieval cue (the contents of the circular aperture), attention was not explicitly drawn to it because the item was presented as an integrated whole.

Thus, the lack of a retrieval-practice advantage in Experiment 2 may have reflected unusually effective restudy in which the retrieval cue was highlighted, rather than a failure of retrieval practice to enhance learning.
Put another way, the testing effect in Experiments 1, 3, 5 and 6 may have been driven by focused attention to the cue in the retrieval practice condition, which was absent in restudy.
This would imply that the testing effect is not induced by pattern completion per se, but rather by knowing which part should be associated with the remaining whole.
To evaluate this possibility, we must determine whether drawing attention to the retrieval cue during restudy is sufficient to eliminate the visual testing effect.
Experiment 7 used the same aperture-cued visual memory task as Experiment 1 but modified the restudy condition so that participants were shown information about the future retrieval cue.
During each restudy trial, a black circle was superimposed on the studied object at the location where the aperture cue would later appear at test (Fig. 14).
text.formatted: During each restudy trial, a black circle was superimposed on the studied object at the location where the aperture cue would later appear at test (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_12">14</ref>).

text.text: Thus, both retrieval practice and restudy trials drew attention to the future retrieval cue, whereas only retrieval practice trials required participants to actively retrieve the whole object from partial visual information.
If retrieval practice continues to produce superior memory performance under these conditions, this would suggest that the critical factor is the act of retrieval itself.
Two hundred and forty-two undergraduate students completed the study; 5 were excluded for failing to respond on more than 20% of trials.

One hundred and seventy-five of the participants were female, 61 male, and 1 other; 34 were Hispanic/Latino and 201 not Hispanic/Latino, 2 chose not to answer; 2 were American Indian/Alaskan Native, 22 Asian, 7 black/African American, 196 White, and 10 chose not to answer.
Stimuli were the same meaningful and abstract objects as in Experiment 1 and the same words as in Experiment 2.
However, 2 additional exemplars of each item category were procured, giving 8 exemplars per category.

Four of the 8 exemplars were randomly assigned to visual occlusion-cued retrieval (the half of the experiment that replicated Experiment 1; see Procedure, below) and the other 4 were assigned to be used in word-image pairs with word-cued retrieval (the half of the study that replicated Experiment 2).

Importantly, in the half of the experiment that replicated Experiment 1, during restudy there was always a black circle superimposed over the location where the aperture cue would later appear at final test (Fig. 14).
text.formatted: Importantly, in the half of the experiment that replicated Experiment 1, during restudy there was always a black circle superimposed over the location where the aperture cue would later appear at final test (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_12">14</ref>).

text.text: The experiment was divided into two separate halves.
One half followed the procedure of Experiment 1, i.e., visual occlusion-cued retrieval, and the other half followed the procedure of Experiment 2, i.e., word-image pairs with word-cued retrieval.
Task type (visual occlusion-cued versus word-cued) was administered within subjects, and which task type occurred first was counterbalanced across participants.
To keep the experiment's length under 1 hour despite including both task types, we adjusted some task parameters described below.

After data collection, we discovered a crucial error in the stimulus presentation code for the half of the experiment that replicated Experiment 2 (word-image pairs with word-cued retrieval), for a majority of participants.
This error caused inconsistent pairings of words with images across presentations and substantially impacted performance; therefore, we discarded these data.

The half of the experiment that replicated Experiment 1 was unaffected by the error, and performance on these trials was good, hence here we report data from only the half of the experiment that replicated Experiment 1 (Fig. 15).
text.formatted: The half of the experiment that replicated Experiment 1 was unaffected by the error, and performance on these trials was good, hence here we report data from only the half of the experiment that replicated Experiment 1 (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_13">15</ref>).

text.text: The changes to the task procedure for the visual occlusion-cued task relative to Experiment 1 were as follows.
First, black circles were superimposed over all stimuli in the restudy condition, indicating the position of the aperture cue to be used at final test.
Second, there was no novel condition, so there were only 16 final test trials per block (rather than 24), of which 8 were restudied items and 8 were retrieval practiced items.

Third, one-third of participants saw 5 final test blocks (as in Experiment 1) but with a slightly faster stimulus presentation rate (2.9 seconds rather than 3 seconds for initial study, aperture presentation, holepunch probe presentation, and 0.5 seconds rather than 1 second for all inter-stimulus blank screens), while the other two-thirds of participants saw 4 final test blocks (fewer than in Experiment 1) but with stimulus timing as in Experiment 1 (i.e., 3 seconds per stimulus presentation and 1 second per blank).
Results were qualitatively similar across these two sets of participants, so the data were pooled.

More participants were recruited than in earlier experiments because there were fewer trials per condition than in Experiments 3 through 6 (which each included 8 test blocks), and because our intention had been to look for an interaction between task type and study condition, which may have required more data to detect.
However, we ultimately could not assess the interaction because of the error in the word-image half of the experiment.
We nonetheless report all the data from the correctly executed visual occlusion-cued half of this experiment.
Memory was indexed by d', as shown in Fig. 15.
text.formatted: Memory was indexed by d', as shown in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_13">15</ref>.

text.text: A two-way [2x2] repeated-measures ANOVA with within-subjects factors Study Condition (restudy, retrieval practice) and Stimulus Type (meaningful, abstract) revealed a main effect of Study Condition, F(1,236) = 4.85, p = 0.029, η²p = 0.020, with a main effect of Stimulus Type, F(1,236) = 26.21, p < 0.001, η²p = .100, and no significant interaction between Study Condition and Stimulus Type, F(1,236) = 0.024, p = 0.88.
text.formatted: A two-way [2x2] repeated-measures ANOVA with within-subjects factors Study Condition (restudy, retrieval practice) and Stimulus Type (meaningful, abstract) revealed a main effect of Study Condition, F(1,236) = 4.85, p = 0.029, η²p = 0.020, with a main effect of Stimulus Type, F(1,236) = 26.21, p < 0.001, η²p = .100, and no significant interaction between Study Condition and Stimulus Type, F(1,236) = 0.024, p = 0.88.

text.text: Given that there was no novel condition, the main effect of Study Condition constitutes evidence for a benefit of retrieval practice over restudy.
These results demonstrate that the visual testing effect persists even when information about the future retrieval cue is provided during restudy.
In fact, in the present experiment, many factors combine to stack the deck in favor of an effect of restudy, making the presence of a testing effect remarkable.

First, as in all of our experiments, participants continued to give pleasantness ratings in the restudy condition, which in some cases are as effective as retrieval practice for encouraging encoding (Whiffen & Karpicke, 2017).
text.formatted: First, as in all of our experiments, participants continued to give pleasantness ratings in the restudy condition, which in some cases are as effective as retrieval practice for encouraging encoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Whiffen & Karpicke, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the black circles overlaid on the stimuli during restudy provided an experience almost akin to pattern completion: to the extent that participants switch their focus of attention from inside the black circle to outside it, the procedure provides sequential, part-to-part exposure much like the aperture followed by feedback in the retrieval practice condition.

Third, in this scenario, there is effectively no delay between viewing the aperture and viewing its surround (only the time it takes for a saccade); thus, this procedure might be expected to engender better aperture-tosurround learning than the retrieval practice condition in which there is a delay between aperture cue and whole-object feedback.
Fourth, the black circle creates brief discontinuities in the contours of the whole object image (Fig. 14), providing localized visual occlusion of the sort that we hypothesize drives learning.
text.formatted: Fourth, the black circle creates brief discontinuities in the contours of the whole object image (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_12">14</ref>), providing localized visual occlusion of the sort that we hypothesize drives learning.

text.text: Thus, in this paradigm, to observe as we did a significant advantage of retrieval practice over restudy attests to the power of retrieval in driving learning.

Given this finding, the retrieval-practice advantage in Experiments 1, 3, 5 and 6 cannot be attributed to retrieval practice merely providing differential information about, or increased attention to, the cue.
Furthermore, these findings render unlikely the possibility that the lack of a testing effect in Experiment 2 was caused by the presence of retrieval-relevant cue information during restudy.
Instead, the visual testing effect appears to depend on the act of retrieval itself.

We tested the hypothesis that visual pattern completion -specifically, part-to-whole retrieval induced by visual occlusion, like recognizing a bicycle behind a picket fence -is a powerful driver of visual learning.

To do so, we employed a novel visual learning paradigm that exploits occlusion-based retrieval along with a match/mismatch test protocol that pairs targets with highly similar lures so that the utility of non-visual, conceptual information is minimized.

Across multiple behavioral experiments, we found a robust visual testing effect -an advantage of retrieval practice over restudy -whenever we employed visual occlusion induced retrieval and used the same visual cue at retrieval practice and final test.
When we removed visual occlusion, the testing effect was no longer present.
Furthermore, we manipulated the level of semantic information that the stimuli contained, pitting meaningful, nameable objects against meaningless, abstract items.

Dialing down the ability of the stimuli to engage semantic representations in this way had no effect on the size of the learning advantage, except in Experiment 5 where we found a greater testing effect for abstract than meaningful items.
Taken together, our findings provide evidence that visual pattern completion serves not only as a retrieval mechanism, but also as a reliable and potent means of enhancing visual learning.
These results also provide the most robust demonstration to date of a testing effect for purely visual information.

In addition, we hypothesized that the pattern completion process that unfolds from the cue is directional: learning accrues to the links between one feature and the next in a direction dictated by the temporal order in which features are "completed".
This leads to the prediction that our visual occlusion recall paradigm should result in learning specific to the cue that is supplied.
This is what we found: the visual testing effect was repeatedly obtained under circumstances using visual occlusion, but not when a different cue was used between retrieval practice and final test.

A similar cue-specific retrieval practice benefit was previously found with verbal stimuli, as predicted by a model proposing intra-item verbal learning analogous to the visual intra-item learning observed here (Hopper & Huber, 2018).
text.formatted: A similar cue-specific retrieval practice benefit was previously found with verbal stimuli, as predicted by a model proposing intra-item verbal learning analogous to the visual intra-item learning observed here <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hopper & Huber, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This result therefore suggests a novel parallel between retrieval-based mechanisms of verbal learning and visual learning.
These findings represent the first empirical demonstration of learning from occlusionbased visual retrieval.

The task bears some resemblance to the fragment-completion or incomplete-picture tasks previously employed in both healthy participants and amnesic patients (e.g., Gabrieli et al., 1994; Gollin, 1960; Milner et al., 1968).
text.formatted: The task bears some resemblance to the fragment-completion or incomplete-picture tasks previously employed in both healthy participants and amnesic patients (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Gabrieli et al., 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Gollin, 1960;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Milner et al., 1968)</ref>.

text.text: However, those tasks differed in several fundamental ways from the peephole-cued recall task introduced here: they required verbal responses (providing the common names of visual items) such that access to conceptual representations was necessary for good performance; they involved no initial study of the specific objects, such that performance at least on early trials drew on general visual knowledge ("perceptual guessing") rather than retrieval of specific visual memories; and, most importantly, they did not compare the efficacy of retrieval practice to the efficacy of whole-item exposure, so it is unknown whether the observed learning was driven by the act of retrieval or simply by repeated exposure to the (gradually more complete) images.
Thus, those studies did not ascertain whether retrieval practice specifically, for visual information alone, enhanced learning.
The present findings have implications for theories of the testing effect.
Several influential accounts of the testing effect propose that it is driven by semantic mediation.

For example, elaborative retrieval theories propose that retrieving an item allows learners to activate and integrate semantic features, generating richer cues for future recall (Carpenter, 2009; Pyc & Rawson, 2010).
text.formatted: For example, elaborative retrieval theories propose that retrieving an item allows learners to activate and integrate semantic features, generating richer cues for future recall <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Carpenter, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Pyc & Rawson, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: A related proposal suggests that retrieval strengthens memory traces by integrating them with preexisting semantic knowledge, effectively consolidating the memory into conceptual networks (Antony et al., 2017; Ferreira & Wimber, 2023).
text.formatted: A related proposal suggests that retrieval strengthens memory traces by integrating them with preexisting semantic knowledge, effectively consolidating the memory into conceptual networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Antony et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Ferreira & Wimber, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Such theories make two predictions germane to the present study: first, if a memory task eliminates the utility of verbalconceptual representations, a testing effect should not be obtained, and second, if an experimenter manipulates the level of pre-existing, semantic information possessed by the stimuli, the testing effect should be diminished when semantic content is reduced.
Our results therefore present a challenge to this theoretical approach.
In contrast to these semantic mediation theories, other theories propose that the learning mechanism underlying the testing effect domain is domain general.

For example, contextual theories propose that retrieval practice updates stored contextual representations, increasing the overlap between practice and test contexts and thereby enhancing later retrieval (Karpicke et al., 2014).
text.formatted: For example, contextual theories propose that retrieval practice updates stored contextual representations, increasing the overlap between practice and test contexts and thereby enhancing later retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Karpicke et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Another theory that eschews a role for semantics is the PCR model of Hopper and Huber (2018), which claims pattern completion plays a key role in the testing effect.
text.formatted: Another theory that eschews a role for semantics is the PCR model of <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hopper and Huber (2018)</ref>, which claims pattern completion plays a key role in the testing effect.

text.text: According to this theory, intra-item learning occurs when pattern completion is induced by providing part of a memory as a cue.
That is, the act of reconstructing the missing features of an item via pattern completion not only retrieves the representation but also modifies and strengthens it.

If such inferential reconstruction causes learning as this theory predicts, then provided that retrieval engages part-to-whole pattern completion, a testing effect should emerge for both semantically rich stimuli and abstract visual stimuli, and that testing effect should not be smaller for the latter.

In support of the domain general PCR model, we repeatedly obtained a visual testing effect in a paradigm employing visual occlusion, even though the utility of conceptual information or verbal labels was effectively eliminated.

As predicted by the PCR model, this part-to-whole learning from visual occlusion was cue-specific and the learning advantage was not greater for stimuli that could be expected to tap representations with greater semantic content.
Moreover, when part-to-whole pattern completion was not involved because we removed visual occlusion, a testing effect was no longer obtained.

Two previous studies that attempted to find a testing effect for abstract visual items failed to do so (Ferreira & Wimber, 2023; McCarter et al., 2025); the present findings suggest that one reason for this failure may be that those paradigms did not encourage visual pattern completion.
text.formatted: Two previous studies that attempted to find a testing effect for abstract visual items failed to do so <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Ferreira & Wimber, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">McCarter et al., 2025)</ref>; the present findings suggest that one reason for this failure may be that those paradigms did not encourage visual pattern completion.

text.text: Interestingly, we repeatedly found a retrieval practice advantage that was the same size or larger for abstract items than for meaningful objects.

In the five studies that found a testing effect, there was either no difference in the testing effect between stimulus types (Experiments 1, 3, 6 and 7), or an interaction that was driven by a larger testing effect for abstract than meaningful items (Experiment 5).
One possibility is that there was a relative retrieval practice advantage for abstract objects owing to participants' tacit (but unhelpful) use of verbal labels for meaningful objects.

That is, if participants invoked a verbal label such as "red lawnmower," they may have experienced verbal overshadowing in which a prototype of a "red lawnmower" came to mind and interfered with discriminating between the two specific lawnmowers that were pitted against each other on a given trial (Dodson et al., 1997; Schooler, 2002; Schooler & Engstler-Schooler, 1990).
text.formatted: That is, if participants invoked a verbal label such as "red lawnmower," they may have experienced verbal overshadowing in which a prototype of a "red lawnmower" came to mind and interfered with discriminating between the two specific lawnmowers that were pitted against each other on a given trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Dodson et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Schooler, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Schooler & Engstler-Schooler, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Under this explanation, verbal overshadowing causes participants to retain the gist ("a red and black manual lawnmower") and lose the specific visual details.

Experiment 5 employed a 6AFC match/mismatch judgment at final test, and it is possible that the simultaneous presentation of six exemplars of the same verbal label exacerbated the verbal overshadowing effect, diminishing the testing effect for meaningful items.

In any testing effect paradigm, it is important to distinguish between a direct testing effect (improved memory for the tested material, i.e., a benefit of the retrieval process itself) and a forward testing effect (improved memory for material encountered following a test, i.e., testpotentiated learning) (Arnold & McDermott, 2013; Gereau & Mulligan, 2026).
text.formatted: In any testing effect paradigm, it is important to distinguish between a direct testing effect (improved memory for the tested material, i.e., a benefit of the retrieval process itself) and a forward testing effect (improved memory for material encountered following a test, i.e., testpotentiated learning) <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arnold & McDermott, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gereau & Mulligan, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The present task offers two possible opportunities for test-potentiated learning.

First, it used retrieval practice trials interleaved with restudy trials within each block, as well as sets of final test trials interposed between study phases across blocks, such that testing frequently preceded subsequent study.
This could have produced test-potentiated new learning (Chan et al., 2018), benefitting any material encountered for the first time after a test.
text.formatted: This could have produced test-potentiated new learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chan et al., 2018)</ref>, benefitting any material encountered for the first time after a test.

text.text: However, this is unlikely to be the main driver of the currently observed testing effect, because the order of presentation of retrieval practice and restudy rounds was counterbalanced and an equal number of retrieval-practiced versus restudied items were presented in each block, so any such effect would boost learning equally for laterintroduced retrieval versus restudy items.

The second opportunity for test-potentiated learning stems from the feedback at retrieval practice: participants see the correct whole item briefly after each retrieval practice trial, providing a test-potentiated encoding opportunity.

However, if this were the sole driver of the testing effect, then we would also have observed a testing effect in Experiments 2 and 4, where the same test-feedback protocol was used but another key task feature -the use of a consistent, occlusion-based cue -was removed; we did not finding a testing effect in either case.

Further attesting to the ineffectiveness of test-potentiated learning in this setting, we previously conducted six visual learning experiments with a similar task and the same test-feedback procedure (but without visual occlusion), and in none did we find a retrieval practice advantage (McCarter et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Further attesting to the ineffectiveness of test-potentiated learning in this setting, we previously conducted six visual learning experiments with a similar task and the same test-feedback procedure (but without visual occlusion), and in none did we find a retrieval practice advantage <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(McCarter et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Another concern in testing effect paradigms can be whether total exposure time is equated across restudy and retrieval practice conditions.

In this task, this is ambiguous because exposure time on retrieval trials differed for different elements of the studied object and because the exposure duration differed (and is difficult to compare) for match versus mismatch trials.

Specifically, when tallying up total exposure to each part of the image for retrieval practice "match" trials, participants saw the aperture in isolation for 3 s and the remainder of the image for 3 s during the match decision, followed by the whole image for 1 s.
Thus, for match trials, each part of the whole image (aperture cue and target "holepunch") was seen for 4 s in total, which is one second longer than for the restudy condition.
In contrast, for "mismatch" trials, although the aperture elements of the object were seen for 4 s in total, the remainder of the image (the target holepunch) was seen for only 1 s during feedback.

If what matters is exposure to the aperture, this favors retrieval practice (4 s for retrieval practice versus 3 s for restudy), but importantly, a correct answer is not possible based on visual familiarity of the aperture cue.

Instead, what likely matters most is exposure to the remainder of the image -i.e., exposure to the target holepunch answer -and this favors restudy (2.5 s on average across match and mismatch retrieval trials versus 3 s for restudy).

Furthermore, even if exposure time for the aperture were the more important factor (although it is not clear why this would be the case under an account in terms of simple exposure), which would suggest an exposure advantage for retrieval practice trials, this advantage should be offset by the fact that, on mismatch trials, participants were exposed to the wrong "holepunch" image (the lure, not the target) for 3s, providing interference.
This discussion highlights the ambiguous nature of exposure time differences and their relative benefits to restudy versus retrieval practice.

However, in the present study this discussion may be moot, because if an imbalance in exposure were the driving force behind the retrieval practice advantage, we should also have observed a testing effect in Experiment 2, in Experiment 4, and in five of the prior experiments of McCarter et al. (2025): all of these studies entailed the same ambiguous imbalance owing to a retrieval practice sequence containing a cue, a match and/or mismatch test item, and a feedback image.

text.text: In total across this study and the study of McCarter et al., 12 experiments have contained this design and yet only 5 have produced a visual testing effect.
text.formatted: In total across this study and the study of <ref type="bibr">McCarter et al.,</ref> <ref type="bibr">12</ref> experiments have contained this design and yet only 5 have produced a visual testing effect.

text.text: The feature those 5 experiments have in common, which is not shared with the 7 failures, is the use of occlusion-based recall with a consistent cue.

In sum, we have provided evidence for a robust new form of visual learning, in which a mechanism long known to underpin retrieval -pattern completion -also underpins encoding, via the strengthening of intra-item, part-to-part associations within visual objects.

This form of visual learning depends on eliciting part-to-whole retrieval via visual occlusion, is specific to the cue that triggers pattern completion, does not require semantic content, is not influenced by the level of semantic content that is available, and produces a memory enhancement that generalizes to novel test formats.
The superiority of this learning mechanism over simple restudy establishes it as an example of a testing effect, in the visual domain.
Furthermore, this discovery draws a novel and fundamental parallel between verbal and visual memory.

Whereas many theories claim that the testing effect requires semantic mediation or elaboration (Antony et al., 2017; Carpenter, 2009; Ferreira & Wimber, 2023; Pyc & Rawson, 2010), restricting it largely to the verbal or semantic domain, our findings suggest that a similar retrieval-induced learning mechanismpattern completion -may apply to both verbal and visual stimuli.
text.formatted: Whereas many theories claim that the testing effect requires semantic mediation or elaboration <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Antony et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Carpenter, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Ferreira & Wimber, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Pyc & Rawson, 2010)</ref>, restricting it largely to the verbal or semantic domain, our findings suggest that a similar retrieval-induced learning mechanismpattern completion -may apply to both verbal and visual stimuli.

text.text: Given that pre-existing semantic knowledge does not enhance this visual testing effect, and that the learning happens in as little as two or three presentations, we suggest that rapid learning of low-level visual representations, which likely takes place in visual cortex, can share many properties with the learning of high-level associations elicited in verbal memory paradigms.
Future neuroimaging work to elucidate the neural bases of these learning effects will allow a more direct test of this conjecture.

section.header: Our primary goal was to ask whether visual pattern completion promotes visual learning.
University of Colorado Boulder institutional review board.
EXPERIMENT 1: DOES PATTERN COMPLETION-BASED RETRIEVAL PRACTICE ENHANCE VISUAL LEARNING?
EXPERIMENT 2: IS VISUAL OCCLUSION REQUIRED TO ELICIT A LEARNING ADVANTAGE?
EXPERIMENT 3: FURTHER REDUCING SEMANTIC KNOWLEDGE OF THE STIMULI
EXPERIMENT 4: DOES THE LEARNING ADVANTAGE TRANSFER TO OTHER PART-TO-WHOLE ASSOCIATIONS?
EXPERIMENT 5: DOES PATTERN-COMPLETION INDUCED LEARNING GENERALIZE TO OTHER TEST FORMATS?
EXPERIMENT 6: IS THERE AN ALTERNATIVE INTERFERENCE-BASED EXPLANATION OF THE VISUAL TESTING EFFECT?
EXPERIMENT 7: DOES THE VISUAL TESTING EFFECT PERSIST WHEN THE RETRIEVAL CUE IS EXPLICITLY PROVIDED DURING RESTUDY?
